analysis.one_liner: Requires nearly all employers to let workers earn up to two weeks of paid vacation a year.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its March 2024 introduction it was sent to five House committees and sat there until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require almost every employer in the country — including federal, state, and congressional employers — to let workers earn one hour of paid leave for every 25 hours worked, up to 80 hours a year. Workers could use the time for any reason, would not have to explain why, would be paid their normal rate while on leave, and would get cash for unused leave when they leave a job. The bill makes it illegal to fire or punish someone for using the leave, and lets workers sue employers who violate it. It never received a hearing or a vote in any committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at virtually all employers, including tipped restaurant and hotel workers, who currently get no paid vacation. Full-time workers would earn about two weeks of paid leave a year; part-time and newer workers earn less but start accruing from day one and can use it after 60 days. Tipped workers on leave must be paid at least the applicable minimum wage. Workers who quit or are fired must be paid for unused leave.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid vacation, especially tipped and part-time workers

how_it_helps.text: Employers must provide 1 hour of paid leave for every 25 hours worked, capped at 80 hours in a 12-month period, with accrual starting at the beginning of employment and use allowed starting on the 60th calendar day of employment.

Leave can be used for any reason, the employer may not require the worker to disclose why, and the employer cannot count the leave against no-fault attendance policies or use taking leave as a negative factor in hiring, promotion, shifts, or discipline.
Tipped employees using leave must be paid at the highest applicable federal, state, or municipal minimum wage, and any employee must be paid at their normal rate for hours they would have worked.
When an employee separates from the employer, the employer must financially reimburse all unused paid leave; if rehired within 12 months, previously earned leave is reinstated.

The bill creates a private right of action with attorney's fees, gives the Labor Department investigative and subpoena authority under the Fair Labor Standards Act framework, and prohibits retaliation against workers who file complaints or testify.
Existing collective bargaining agreements or benefit plans with more generous leave are preserved, and no contract can give workers less than the bill's minimum.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — from one-employee businesses to major corporations — bear the cost of paying wages for leave not worked, of paying out unused leave at separation, and of recordkeeping and notice duties. Workers may face some indirect effects if employers respond by reducing hiring or hours.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers of all sizes, including small businesses

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a direct new cost on employers, who must pay wages for time not worked and pay out unused leave at separation, with no small-business exemption — the bill covers employers with as few as one employee.
Tipped workers who take leave earn the minimum wage rather than their usual earnings including tips, so their leave time can pay less than a working day would.

Employers may require up to two weeks' advance notice and may refuse a specific scheduling request for a bona fide business reason, so workers do not get unconditional control over when leave is taken.
The bill excludes sick leave and Family and Medical Leave Act leave from the definition of paid annual leave, so it adds vacation only and does not address medical or caregiving leave.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is broad and concrete: a guaranteed, enforceable right to paid time off for workers who currently have none, with anti-retaliation teeth and a private right of action. The costs are real but are the standard tradeoff of any leave mandate — employers pay for leave not worked, and small businesses with thin margins feel it most, and the tipped-worker pay rule is a genuine design flaw. On balance the bill's benefits flow to millions of workers while its costs are spread across the employer community.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to five House committees on the same day, and no committee ever held a hearing or vote on it; it died there when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on March 20, 2024, with 42 original cosponsors.

The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Education and Workforce, Oversight and Accountability, House Administration, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Judiciary Committees, each for consideration of provisions within its jurisdiction.
Cosponsorship grew to 53 House members, all Democrats.
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a committee vote, a hearing listed in the record, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid for guaranteed vacation come out ahead, since no leave mandate was enacted; workers without paid leave gained nothing. The bill's 54 House Democratic supporters ended the Congress with nothing enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided a paid-leave mandate

sides.party_line_note: All 54 supporters — the sponsor and 53 cosponsors — were House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor, and with Republicans holding a 224-seat House majority the bill never advanced out of any committee or received a vote.

industries.industry: Employers across the economy (retail, restaurants, hospitality, services)
industries.note: The bill requires paying wages for leave not worked and cashing out unused leave at separation, with no small-business exemption — the employer's interest in avoiding that cost runs directly against workers gaining paid leave.
Their tipped staff must be paid at least the applicable minimum wage while on leave, and the bill bars requiring workers to find shift coverage as a condition of taking leave.

industries.industry: Government employers (federal agencies, state programs, congressional offices)
industries.note: State and congressional employers are covered, and states accepting federal financial assistance would effectively waive immunity to suits by their employees under the bill; federal workers themselves would gain the same leave entitlement.
